title: Singleness: A Bible Study for the Unmarried
subtitle: A five-session study on singleness, calling, and belonging.
summary:
This study is for single people: the never-married, the widowed and the divorced, those who chose singleness and those who didn't. It's also for the small groups and churches that have too often left them standing in the lobby. Its five sessions take up singleness as a calling rather than a deficiency; desire and loneliness, which nobody should be shamed for feeling; chastity as honor for a body that is good; the church as a family wider than the nuclear household; and contentment and the fruit a single life can bear. A volunteer can lead it without preparation. Each question carries a note for the leader, and each session ends in prayer.

The church has largely been built around couples and families: the sermon series on marriage, the family potluck, the couples' small group. Single people have often been left to feel that the meeting hasn't started yet. I'm a pastor, and this study doesn't point at that from a safe distance; pastors built those churches. It lets the single voices of Scripture carry the weight: Jesus, Paul and Jeremiah. It won't treat singleness as a lesser Christianity or a holding pattern. It will honor the person content in it and sit beside the person aching in it, and it won't tell either one that they're half of something waiting to be completed.
audience: Single adults, the widowed and divorced, and the churches and groups that carry them

sessions.title: A Calling, Not a Deficiency
sessions.aim: To see singleness as a calling Scripture honors and Jesus himself lived, not a deficiency waiting to be cured by marriage, while taking seriously the good of marriage and the longing for it.
sessions.summary:
Many single adults, seated once again at the back table of someone else's wedding, begin to feel like a problem the church doesn't know how to solve. They've picked up, in a hundred small ways, the message that the single life is a phase on the way to the real thing.

So the question isn't only whether singleness is hard. It's what singleness is, because a deficiency is something you try to cure and a calling is something you steward. Paul calls singleness a gift, the same word he uses for gifts of the Spirit, and wishes more people had it (1 Corinthians 7:7). And the single person Scripture holds highest is Jesus, whom nobody would call incomplete. The strong case on the other side is real: God said it isn't good for the man to be alone (Genesis 2:18), and marriage is part of creation's design. But that word was never a promise that marriage is the only answer to being alone. The New Testament opens a calling Eden couldn't yet see.

keyScripture.why: Paul calls both marriage and singleness gifts from God. He doesn't rank the single life beneath the married one, and he wishes more people shared his own.

discussion.q: Where have you picked up the message that the single life is a phase you pass through on the way to the real thing? What did it do to how you saw your life?
discussion.behind: Start with experience before theology. Single people have absorbed this through seating charts, sermon illustrations that assume a spouse, and questions about settling down. Let the married people in the room hear how loudly the church has said something it never meant to say.

discussion.q: Jesus never married, and nobody calls his life incomplete. What changes when you let that register?
discussion.behind: Most people have never stopped to notice it. If singleness were a deficiency, the life of Jesus would make no sense. The point isn't to win an argument but to take pressure off: singleness isn't a lack Jesus came to fix but a life he shared.

discussion.q: Read Genesis 2:18. God said it isn't good for the man to be alone. What's true in the view that marriage is the creation design, and what don't you want to lose?
discussion.behind: Protect both the argument and the person who aches. Marriage is a real good, not a consolation prize, and the study must never sound as if it's talking anyone out of wanting it. Honor the design and the desire before showing what the New Testament adds.

discussion.q: Read 1 Corinthians 7:7-8. If singleness is a calling to steward and not a deficiency to cure, what would it look like to build a life on it rather than wait for one to begin?
discussion.behind: Move from diagnosis to imagination. The waiting-room posture keeps people from putting down roots: buying the house, taking the job, making the home their own. Don't let it become a pep talk.

discussion.q: Single or married, where have you treated singleness as the lesser state?
discussion.behind: Answer first. Single people often believe the diminishment about themselves more deeply than anyone imposes it. Married people often assume, without any malice, that their arrangement is where everyone is headed. Name it gently.

objections.objection: God himself said it isn't good for the man to be alone. Marriage is the design and singleness the exception, so calling them equally good just flatters people who haven't found a spouse.
objections.response: There's real truth here, and it deserves to be granted fully. Marriage is a creation good, not a consolation prize, and the longing for it echoes a real design. Nobody should be made to feel foolish for that ache. But the objection assumes something Scripture doesn't say: that marriage is the only answer to the aloneness God named. That word was spoken into a world with two people in it, before there was a covenant people, a church or a resurrection. Jesus was unmarried and not alone. Paul, unmarried, calls his state a gift. The creation word is true. It was never a decree that marriage is a single person's only way out of being alone, because the deepest belonging was always meant to be found in God and his people, and marriage is a sign of that, not its source.

objections.objection: Single people in the church are just people who haven't found anyone yet. Calling it a holy calling makes a disappointment sound spiritual.
objections.response: This names something the church's cheerful language often covers up: for many people singleness isn't chosen, and it carries real disappointment. Pretending otherwise is its own cruelty. But a calling isn't the same as a preference. Jeremiah didn't choose the singleness God gave him (Jeremiah 16:1-2), and Paul didn't choose his thorn. A calling can be one you didn't ask for and still be from God, and still bear fruit. The disappointment is real, and so is the calling. Naming the second doesn't deny the first.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What have you told yourself you'll do once you're married, and what would it mean to begin it now, as if this life were already your real one?
sessions.practice: Name one place you've lived as though your real life were still ahead of you: roots you haven't put down, work you haven't taken, a home you haven't made your own. Take one concrete step this week to plant something there. And whether you're single or married, ask God privately where you've believed singleness is a lesser life, and write down what comes to mind.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, you made us for belonging, and in your Son you showed us a single life so full that no one could call it incomplete. Forgive us for teaching, in a hundred quiet ways, that the unmarried life is a waiting room. Forgive the churches that seated single people at the back and called it hospitality. Teach us to receive singleness as Paul did, as a gift and a calling, and teach those of us who are married to see the assumption we never knew we held. Let no one in this room believe they're half of something. In Christ they are whole, and their life has already begun. Amen.
reflection: Where have I believed, or led others to believe, that the single life is a phase rather than a life?
If the fullest human life ever lived was an unmarried one, what does that say about the completeness I expected marriage to give?
What have I put off planting or beginning because I was waiting for marriage to start my life?
sessions.teaching:
Picture a woman in her late thirties at another wedding, seated again at the back table with the other unmarried guests. She isn't bitter, and she isn't exaggerating. She's reporting accurately a message she's received in a hundred small ways: the single life is a phase you pass through on the road to the real thing, and until you get there you're unfinished, a house with the frame up and nobody living in it.

Before we ask whether singleness is hard, which everyone knows, we have to ask what it is, because the answer decides how a person lives it. A deficiency is something you try to cure. A calling is something you steward. Those aren't two moods about the same life. They're two different lives.

Scripture doesn't treat singleness as a deficiency. Paul writes, "I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and one of another" (1 Corinthians 7:7). The word for gift there is the same one he uses for the gifts of the Spirit. And he goes on: "To the unmarried and the widows I say that it is good for them to remain single, as I am" (1 Corinthians 7:8). Not tolerable. Good. Jesus spoke of some who would give up marriage "for the sake of the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 19:12). And then there's the fact that should have settled this long ago. The fullest human life ever lived was an unmarried one. Jesus never married, and in two thousand years nobody has called his life half-finished. Given a whole human life to live, God the Son lived it single.

The strong case on the other side deserves a full hearing, because thoughtful people make it from the text. God said, "It is not good that the man should be alone" (Genesis 2:18). Marriage is written into creation and blessed from the start. I won't have this study talk anyone out of a longing God himself planted. Marriage isn't a consolation prize, and wanting it isn't immaturity.

But the objection assumes something Scripture never says: that marriage is the only cure for the aloneness God named. That word was spoken before there was a covenant people, a church or a resurrection, into a world with exactly two people in it. The rest of the Bible answers it in ways Eden couldn't yet see. Isaiah promises the eunuch, a man with no wife or children, "a name better than sons and daughters" in God's house (Isaiah 56:5). Jesus, unmarried, wasn't alone. The deepest belonging a person can know was always meant to be found in God and his people. Marriage, good as it is, points to that belonging. It was never its source.

This is where I have to stand inside the failure. Pastors have built the church around couples and families. We planned the sermon series on marriage, the seminar on parenting and the couples' small group, and without ever deciding to, we put single people at the back of our imagination. We made the potluck a family event and the retreat a couples' getaway, then wondered why unmarried members drifted. We treated their singleness, without a word, as something we hoped God would fix. I can't teach this from above it.

For Paul, the single life wasn't the waiting room before the Christian life. It was the Christian life, freed for the kingdom in a way he says marriage isn't. For some people in this room it isn't a delay or a problem to solve. It's the whole house, built on purpose, by the same God who gave his own Son a single life to live. That life isn't waiting to begin. It's already underway. The church is the one that has been slow to honor it.

scriptureStudy.note: "It is not good that the man should be alone." The word names a real need for belonging. It's spoken before covenant, church or resurrection, and the rest of Scripture answers it with more than marriage.
"Each has his own gift from God." Paul calls both singleness and marriage gifts and refuses to rank them. Singleness isn't the lack of one gift; it's a gift of its own.
"It is good for them to remain single, as I am." Good, not second-best. And Paul includes the widowed, whose singleness came through loss.
Some "have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven." Jesus honors a singleness taken up for the kingdom and says, "Let the one who is able to receive this receive it."
To the eunuchs who keep his Sabbaths, God promises "a monument and a name better than sons and daughters." Descendants aren't the measure of a life in God's house.
"You shall not take a wife." God called Jeremiah to a singleness he didn't choose, as a sign to his people. A calling can be hard and unchosen and still come from God.
No one who has left house or wife or family for the kingdom "will not receive many times more in this time, and in the age to come eternal life." What's given up for the kingdom isn't lost.

sessions.goingDeeper:
The church hasn't always treated singleness the way much of the modern church does. For long stretches of Christian history the single life was held in high honor, sometimes too high. By the late fourth century, writers like Jerome praised virginity so far above marriage that Augustine wrote On the Good of Marriage (about 401) partly to defend marriage's dignity. A group should grant that the overcorrection was real.

Then the Reformation recovered the honor of marriage. Luther's The Estate of Marriage (1522) is an example. That recovery was right and needed. But over time much of the Protestant world swung so far that it kept almost no positive vision of singleness, until the unmarried Christian was simply someone waiting. Set that beside the plain fact that Jesus and Paul were both single, and that the early church spread partly through unmarried men and women free to go where a family couldn't follow.

Then a harder question. Our wider culture tends to treat romantic partnership as the center of a meaningful life. That isn't a Christian idea, but the church has often absorbed it without noticing. Ask where that assumption got into your own church, and whom it has quietly hurt.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a single man in his forties, settled, faithful and useful in the church, stiffens when this session calls singleness a calling. He says he doesn't want his singleness called a gift. He's prayed for marriage for twenty years, and "calling" sounds like being told to be grateful for something he grieves.

Honor him before you press anything. He's right that the church sometimes uses the word "calling" to shut down a real grief; say so and mean it. His longing isn't a lack of faith. But notice his assumption that a calling only counts if you chose it. Scripture is full of callings nobody asked for, Jeremiah's singleness among them. Naming his life a calling doesn't deny his grief. It dignifies it, because a gift he didn't choose can still come from God and still bear fruit.

Don't let the conversation collapse into whether he's happy about it. Honor the grief fully, and then ask gently whether the years he's called wasted might be years God has been working through.

sessions.title: Desire, Loneliness, and the Honest Ache
sessions.aim: To make room for the real ache of singleness, the desire for a spouse and the loneliness of life without one, without shaming the person who feels it or pretending faith makes it vanish, and to recover lament as the way between false cheer and despair.
sessions.summary:
Single people who admit they're lonely are often told they just need to be content in Christ, as though the loneliness were a sin to confess rather than a wound to meet. That pressure to pretend may hurt more than any seating chart.

Two lies compete for the single heart. One says the ache means your faith is weak. The other says the ache is the final truth about your life. The first has a real truth behind it: Scripture does command contentment, and Paul learned it (Philippians 4:11-12). Turning a longing over and over can become its own bondage. But contentment isn't the absence of ache. The Psalms are full of faithful people telling God how much it hurts, and Jesus in Gethsemane said, "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death" (Matthew 26:38). There's a third way, older than both lies: lament, which tells God the truth about the pain and keeps reaching for him with it.

keyScripture.why: "Pour out your heart before him." The way between denial and despair is to bring the whole heart, ache and all, to a God who is a refuge, not a judge of our pain.

discussion.q: Have you felt pressure to pretend the ache isn't there? What happened to it when you had to hide it?
discussion.behind: Go gently; some people in the room have never been allowed to say this aloud. Performing contentment doesn't remove loneliness. It pushes it underground. Make the room safe first, and go first if the silence is heavy.

discussion.q: One lie says the ache means your faith has failed. The other says the ache is the whole truth about your life. Which has had more power over you?
discussion.behind: Some people are crushed by guilt for feeling lonely at all. Others have accepted loneliness as a verdict. Naming which voice is loudest is the first step toward answering it.

discussion.q: Read Philippians 4:11-12. What's true in the call to contentment, and where does it get twisted into a command to feel no pain?
discussion.behind: Hold both. Contentment is real and commanded, and endless brooding can become bondage; the study mustn't excuse self-pity. But contentment isn't the absence of ache, and Scripture holds the two together without strain.

discussion.q: Read Psalm 42:1-3 and Matthew 26:36-39. What would change if you brought your loneliness to God as lament instead of hiding it as a failure?
discussion.behind: Most of us have lost the language of lament. The Psalms model prayer that tells God the plain truth and still addresses him. Help the room see that God isn't fragile in front of their ache.

discussion.q: Read Psalm 73:25-26. Where might your deepest longing be pointing past what you want toward the God you need?
discussion.behind: This isn't a trick to make the desire for marriage disappear by renaming it. Every earthly longing finally points past itself. Let the desire be honored and turned toward God at once, and end there, without tying it off.

objections.objection: If I'm supposed to be content in Christ, then still being lonely and still wanting to be married must mean my faith is weak.
objections.response: That fear does real damage, and it doesn't come from God. Nowhere does Scripture teach that faith removes desire or that a holy person feels no ache. The psalmists told God, at length, how much their lives hurt. Jesus, the only person with perfect faith, was "very sorrowful, even to death" in the garden and didn't pretend otherwise (Matthew 26:38). If perfect faith didn't erase the ache in him, expecting your faith to erase it in you isn't humility. It's a burden Scripture never lays on anyone. The contentment Paul learned isn't the absence of longing. It's God's presence inside the longing. Bring the ache to him. That isn't weak faith. It's where faith lives.

objections.objection: Telling me my loneliness points to God is a way of spiritualizing a real problem. I don't want a lesson. I want another person who won't leave.
objections.response: There's a lot of truth in this. Wanting another human being who won't leave is good and God-given, and private devotion isn't a full substitute for someone in the next room. But the objection assumes a choice Scripture doesn't make, between God and people. Scripture answers loneliness with God and a people: "God settles the solitary in a home" (Psalm 68:6), and the church is meant to be a real, embodied family, which session four takes up. The dodge isn't saying that God meets you. The dodge is a church that says so and then fails to be the family through which he does.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What ache have you hidden, even from God, because you were afraid that feeling it meant your faith had failed?
sessions.practice: This week, take your loneliness and longing to God directly, out loud or on paper, the way the psalmists did, without first editing it into something more spiritual. Don't try to resolve it; just bring it. If you've been carrying it alone, tell one person you trust, not to be fixed but to be known. Write down what changes when the ache is spoken instead of buried.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, you made us to long, and you told us we could bring our longing to you without shame. Forgive the church for teaching single people to hide the ache and call the hiding faith. Teach us the prayer of lament, to tell you how much it hurts and keep reaching for you inside the hurt, as the psalmists did and as your Son did in the garden. Meet the lonely among us with your presence and with a people who will be your hands. And take our deepest longing and turn it home to you. Amen.
reflection: Which lie has been louder in me: that the ache means my faith has failed, or that the ache is the final truth about my life?
Have I ever brought my loneliness to God as lament, or have I only tried to hide it from him?
If every earthly longing points past itself to God, what might my desire for marriage be telling me about the belonging I most need?
sessions.teaching:
The seating chart at a wedding hurts, and so does the bulletin that only speaks to families. But I think the cruelest thing the church does to single people is quieter: the pressure to pretend the ache isn't there. Think of a young man who admits, with some courage, that he's lonely, that the empty apartment presses on him at the end of the day, and is told kindly that he just needs to be content in Christ. The loneliness gets treated as a sin to confess rather than a wound to meet.

So we have to start with the ache itself. Two lies compete for the single heart, and both are cruel. The first says the ache is a failure of faith: a surrendered believer wouldn't feel this, so if you still want to be married and still feel lonely at night, your walk with God must be shallow. That lie lays guilt on top of grief. The second lie says the ache is the whole truth: you're alone and always will be, and loneliness isn't a feeling but a verdict.

The first lie has bent something true, and it deserves a fair hearing. Scripture does command contentment. Paul writes, "I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content. I know how to be brought low, and I know how to abound" (Philippians 4:11-12). Turning a longing over and over until it becomes the center of the self can become a kind of bondage, and brooding isn't the same thing as telling the truth.

But contentment in the Bible is never described as the absence of ache. The same Scripture that commands contentment gives us the Psalms, and around a third of them, by most counts, are laments: faithful people telling God plainly how much their lives hurt. "How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever?" (Psalm 13:1). "My tears have been my food day and night" (Psalm 42:3). These aren't the prayers of weak faith. They're the prayers God gave his people as a model for talking to him about pain. And then there's the garden. Jesus, the only person whose faith was ever perfect, knelt in Gethsemane and said, "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death" (Matthew 26:38). If perfect faith didn't remove the ache from the Son of God, expecting your faith to remove it from you was never humility. It was a weight no one in Scripture was asked to carry.

Here's the turn. The ache isn't the enemy of faith. Often it's the shape faith takes in a heart that longs. Every earthly desire, followed far enough, points past itself. The longing for a spouse who won't leave is real and good, and underneath it is the longing of a creature for the One who never leaves. The psalmist got there by way of honest struggle: "Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you" (Psalm 73:25).

So you don't have to choose between false cheer and despair. There's a third way, older than both, and the church has nearly forgotten it. It's called lament. It tells God the whole truth about the ache and keeps reaching for him with it.

Those of us who are married have often been part of the machinery of the first lie. We've handed a lonely person a verse and a smile when what they needed was for someone to sit with them and let the ache be real. It's easier to fix a feeling than to feel it with someone. The gospel doesn't fix the ache by making it disappear. It meets it with a God who took on a human heart and let it break, and who says, "Trust in him at all times, O people; pour out your heart before him; God is a refuge for us" (Psalm 62:8).

scriptureStudy.note: "Pour out your heart before him; God is a refuge for us." Permission most Christians never claim: to bring the unedited heart to God, who receives it as a refuge.
"My tears have been my food day and night." The psalmist grieves openly, and the grief is kept as inspired prayer. Lament is a form of faith, not a lapse from it.
"My soul is very sorrowful, even to death." Jesus names his anguish in the garden, which undoes the idea that strong enough faith feels no ache.
"I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content." Paul's contentment is learned, not automatic. It's God's presence in the circumstance, not the absence of hard feeling.
"Whom have I in heaven but you?" The psalmist's desire, wrestled through, lands on God as the portion no loss can take.
"God settles the solitary in a home." God takes the loneliness of the solitary as his concern, and in the New Testament the home is the household of his people.
"My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness." Paul's thorn wasn't removed. God often meets an ache not by taking it away but by meeting the person inside it.

sessions.goingDeeper:
Around a third of the Psalms, by most counts, are laments: complaint and grief addressed directly to God. Yet they're largely missing from much contemporary worship, which leans toward the triumphant. A group might ask what that loss has cost. A church with no room for grief will tell its hurting members to cover the pain, and single people carrying an unmet longing are among the first to pay for it.

Then look at the wider culture. In 2000 the sociologist Robert Putnam documented the decline of American civic and community life in Bowling Alone, and in 2023 the U.S. Surgeon General issued an advisory calling loneliness and isolation an epidemic. These accounts name something real: the bonds of family, neighborhood and congregation have frayed. They tend to treat loneliness as a problem to be solved with better connection, which helps. Scripture goes deeper and treats it as the signal of a creature made for belonging with God and with his people. Let the research show the size of the wound and Scripture show its depth, and refuse any comfort that hurries a lonely person past a pain the Bible itself would sit down beside.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a single woman in your group says, a little too quickly, that she's fine, that she gave all this to God years ago and doesn't struggle with it anymore. The room can feel a door close.

Be gentle, and don't pry. She may really be at peace, and assuming every single person is secretly devastated is its own condescension. But a quick "I'm fine" that shuts a conversation down can be the sound of performed contentment. Don't challenge her in front of the group; let what she said stand. Make a private moment available. If she takes it, offer your presence rather than a verse, and let her know that an ache, if it's there, isn't a failure and doesn't need hiding from you or from God.

The aim isn't to produce a grief she doesn't feel. It's to make sure that if it's there, she knows there's a room, and a God, that can hold it.
